title: De Peccato Originali
author: Augustine
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0040.stoa056c.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Attendite itaque quid Caelestius apertissime dixerit, et ibi uidebitis quid uobis Pelagius occultauerit. Caelestius quippe adiungit et dicit: \'in remissionem autem peccatorum baptizandos infantes non idcirco diximus, ut peccatum ex traduce firmare uideamur. quod longe a catholico sensu alienum est, quia peccatum non cum homine nascitur, quod postmodum exercetur ab homine, quia non naturae delictum, sed uoluntatis esse monstratur.
passages.english: Pay attention, then, to what Caelestius said quite openly, and there you will see what Pelagius has hidden from you. For Caelestius adds and says: 'We have not said that infants are to be baptized for the remission of sins in order that we might seem to affirm sin by transmission [ex traduce]. That is far removed from the catholic understanding, because sin, which is afterwards committed by a human being, is not born with the human being, since it is shown to be a fault not of nature but of the will.
passages.notes: 'Peccatum ex traduce': sin transmitted by propagation from the parents (traducianism).

passages.original: quoniam neque per mortem uol praeuaricationem Adae omne genus hominum moriatur neque per resurrectionem Christi omne genus hominum resurgat. quoniam sanctus episcopus Augustinus aduersus discipulos eius in Sicilia respondit Hilario ad subiecta capitula scribens librum in quo ista continentur: posse hominem sine peccato esse, si uelit. infantes, etsi non baptizentur, habere uitam aeternam. diuites baptizatos, nisi omnibus abrenuntient, si quid boni uisi fuerint facere, non reputari illis neque regnum dei posse eos habere, Pelagius dixit: [de] posse quidem hominem sine peccato esse dictum est superius;
passages.english: that neither does the whole human race die through the death or transgression of Adam, nor does the whole human race rise again through the resurrection of Christ. Since the holy bishop Augustine, replying to his disciples in Sicily, wrote to Hilarius on the appended headings a book in which these [points] are contained: that a man can be without sin, if he wishes; that infants, even if they are not baptized, have eternal life; that rich men who have been baptized, unless they renounce everything, are not credited with whatever good they may seem to have done, nor can they possess the kingdom of God, Pelagius said: [Concerning the claim] that a man can indeed be without sin, it has been addressed above;
passages.notes: 'uol' is read as 'uel' (or), a scanning error. The bracketed '[de]' is the edition's own marking. The sentence beginning 'quoniam sanctus episcopus Augustinus' is loosely constructed: it is a charge read out at the synod, introducing further propositions that Augustine had answered. It is rendered as an introductory clause leading into Pelagius' reply.

passages.original: Quomodo autem Pelagius temptarit obrepere ad fallendum etiam apostolicae sedis episcopale iudicium in hac ipsa quaestione de baptismate paruulorum diligenter attendite. in litteris enim quas Romam misit ad beatae memoriae papam Innocentium, quoniam eum in corpore non inuenerunt et sancto papae Zosimo datae sunt atque ad nos inde directae, dicit se ab hominibus infamari, quod neget paruulis baptismi sacramentum et absque redemptione Christi aliquibus caelorum regna promittat.
passages.english: Now pay careful attention to how Pelagius tried to creep in so as to deceive even the episcopal judgment of the apostolic see on this very question of the baptism of little ones. For in the letter which he sent to Rome to Pope Innocent of blessed memory, which, since they did not find him in the body, was given to the holy Pope Zosimus and from there sent on to us, he says that he is defamed by people for supposedly denying the sacrament of baptism to little ones and promising the kingdom of heaven to some without the redemption of Christ.

passages.original: Non igitur sicut Pelagius et eius discipuli tempora diuidamus dicentes \'primum uixisse iustos homines ex natura, deinde sub lege, tertio sub gratia — ex natura, scilicet ab Adam tam longa aetate, qua lex nondum erat data — tunc enim', aiunt, educe ratione cognoscebatur creator et quemadmodum uiuendum esset scriptum gerebatur in cordibus, non lege litterae, sed naturae.
passages.english: Let us not, then, divide the ages as Pelagius and his disciples do, saying 'that righteous people lived first by nature, then under the law, thirdly under grace — by nature, that is, from Adam through that long age in which the law had not yet been given — for at that time', they say, 'the Creator was known by the guidance of reason, and how one ought to live was carried written in hearts, not by the law of the letter, but by that of nature.

passages.original: Sed iam etiam istum conclusuri librum oportere arbitramur, ut Ambrosium antistitem dei, cuius inter latinae linguae scriptores ecclesiasticos praecipue Pelagius integerrimam fidem praedicat, sicut de gratia fecimus ita et de peccato originali, in quo delendo ipsa gratia euidentius commendatur, calumniosae istorum loquacitati respondere faciamus. in eo opere quod scripsit de resurrectione sanctus Ambrosius \'lapsus sum\', inquit, \'in Adam, de paradiso eiectus sum in Adam, mortuus in Adam: quomodo reuocat nisi me in Adam inuenerit ut in illo culpae obnoxium, morti debitum, ita in Christo iustificatum?1 item scribens contra Nouatianos ait: (omnes homines sub peccato nascimur, quorum ipse ortus in uitio est, sicut habes lectum dicente Dauid: ecce in iniquitatibus conceptus sum et in delictis peperit me mater mea. ideo Pauli caro corpus mortis erat, sicut ipse ait: quis me liberabit de corpore mortis huius? Christi autem caro damnauit peccatum, quod nascendo non sensit, quod moriendo crucifixit, ut in carne nostra esset iustificatio per gratiam, ubi erat ante conluuio per culpam\'. item idem ipse cum exponeret Esaiam prophetam, loquens de Christo \'ideo\', inquit, 'et quasi homo per uniuersa temptatus est et in similitudine hominum cuncta sustinuit, sed quasi de spiritu natus abstinuit a peccato; omnis enim homo mendax et nemo sine peccato nisi unus deus.
passages.english: But since we are now about to conclude this book too, we think we ought to make Ambrose, bishop of God, whose wholly sound faith Pelagius proclaims above all among the church writers of the Latin language, answer the slanderous loquacity of these people on original sin, as we did on grace; for in the blotting out of that sin grace itself is the more clearly commended. In the work which he wrote on the resurrection, Saint Ambrose says: 'I fell in Adam, I was cast out of paradise in Adam, I died in Adam: how does he call me back unless he has found me in Adam, so that, as in him I was liable to guilt and owed to death, so in Christ I am justified?' Likewise, writing against the Novatianists, he says: 'All of us human beings are born under sin, and our very origin is in fault, as you have it read when David says: Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me. That is why the flesh of Paul was a body of death, as he himself says: Who will deliver me from the body of this death? But the flesh of Christ condemned sin, which he did not experience in being born, and which he crucified in dying, so that in our flesh there might be justification through grace where before there was filth through guilt.' Likewise the same man, when he was expounding the prophet Isaiah, speaking of Christ, says: 'Therefore, both as a man he was tempted in all things and in the likeness of men he endured all things, but as one born of the Spirit he abstained from sin; for every man is a liar, and no one is without sin except God alone.
passages.notes: The stray '1' after 'iustificatum' is a footnote mark, omitted.

passages.original: His tamen uerbis hominis dei, quem tanto praeconio ipse laudauit Pelagius, contradicit et dicit <sicut sine uirtute ita nos sine uitio procreari\'. quid igitur restat, nisi <ut) aut istum Pelagius suum damnet errorem aut eum sic Ambrosium laudasse paeniteat? sed quia ista secundum catholicam fidem beatus Ambrosius ut episcopus catholicus est locutus, sequitur, ut ab hac uia fidei deuius merito Pelagius cum Caelestio discipulo suo catholicae ecclesiae sit auctoritate damnatus, nisi eum non Ambrosium laudasse, sed contra Ambrosium sensisse paeniteat.
passages.english: Yet Pelagius contradicts these words of the man of God, whom he himself praised with such high commendation, and says 'that we are begotten without vice just as without virtue'. What remains, then, except that Pelagius either condemn this error of his own or regret having praised Ambrose so? But since blessed Ambrose, as a catholic bishop, said these things in accordance with the catholic faith, it follows that Pelagius, straying from this way of faith, has deservedly been condemned, together with his disciple Caelestius, by the authority of the catholic church, unless he regrets, not having praised Ambrose, but having held views against Ambrose.
